## Part 1 – Verse by verse (traditional reading)

**v. 1**
- Ellicott: in time order, this chapter and the next come after chapter 4. He cites Jerome for this. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-7.html
- Gill: dates the vision to Belshazzar's first year, 17 years before Babylon fell. Daniel wrote it down so it wouldn't be lost and future readers could use it, and he gave "the sum," meaning the main points. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-7.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/7.htm
- Wesley: the visions were written for the church, to correct the belief that all would go well once the exiles returned home. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-daniel/
- Matthew Henry: Daniel both wrote and spoke the vision. Henry takes this as a sign that the church is taught by both Scripture and preaching. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_007.cfm
- Constable: this is the first time in the book that a vision is written down. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-7.html

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: the "great sea" here isn't the Mediterranean. Going by v. 17, it stands for the nations of the world. The winds from all four directions picture the political and social unrest that drives history toward its end. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-7.html
- Gill: allows that the sea could be either the Mediterranean or the open ocean. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/7.htm
- Wesley: the winds are rival nations fighting wars, which produce the four beasts one after another. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-daniel/
- Enduring Word: mentions that some writers (Strauss, for example) see the winds as satanic forces, comparing Revelation 7:1. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-7/

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: "great" points to how monstrous the beasts look, not how big they are. They rise one after another, which matches the statue in chapter 2. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-7.html
- Gill: the four beasts are four empires in order: Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome. They are pictured as beasts because of their violence and tyranny. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/7.htm
- Wesley: makes the same identification. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-daniel/
- Precept Austin: chapter 2 shows the empires as people see them, and chapter 7 shows them as God sees them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_7_commentary1
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB): the beasts show worldly kingdoms as less than human because they are cut off from God. Humanity's true dignity is found only in the kingdom of the "Son of man." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Dan/Dan_007.cfm

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: the lion stands for strength and the eagle for speed. Together they picture Nebuchadnezzar's empire, which matches the golden head of the statue. Jerome linked the plucked wings to the king's madness and recovery. Ellicott objects that the vision is about the kingdom, not the king. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-7.html
- Gill: the plucked wings mean Babylon's power shrank under the kings who came after Nebuchadnezzar, as provinces broke away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/7.htm
- Wesley: the "man's heart" means Babylon lost its lion-like courage and became faint-hearted. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-daniel/
- Enduring Word: the beast is Babylon, which suits Nebuchadnezzar's majesty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-7/

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: the bear matches the statue's silver chest and arms. Its two sides stand for an empire made of two parts, with one part (Persia) becoming more prominent. Since Hippolytus, the three ribs have been read as three conquered nations: Babylon, Lydia and Egypt. "Arise, devour" means the empire is allowed further conquests. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-7.html
- Wesley: the bear is the Medes and Persians, and the raised side is the north, because the Medes rose first. The ribs are Babylonian subject peoples who revolted. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-daniel/
- Enduring Word: Medo-Persia, whose huge armies overwhelmed their enemies. Guzik quotes Clarke on the bear's cruelty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-7/
- Matthew Henry: unjust conquests are like a predator's, only worse, because beasts don't prey on their own kind. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_007.cfm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: the animal is really a panther, known for being watchful and fast. The wings are a bird's, not an eagle's, so it is less swift than the first beast. The four heads are the four kingdoms the empire would split into. Ellicott also notes a pattern: one for the first beast, two for the second, four for the third. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-7.html
- Wesley: this is the Greek empire. It began smaller than the lion, just as Alexander fought Darius with a smaller army. The four heads are Alexander's four commanders, who divided the empire. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-daniel/
- Enduring Word: Alexander's rapid conquests and the four-way split are described so precisely that they show God knows the future. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-7/

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: the fourth beast matches the iron of chapter 2, and its ten horns match the statue's ten toes. Whatever it didn't devour, it trampled. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-7.html
- Gill: the beast is Rome. He rejects the views that it is the Turkish empire (Aben Ezra) or the Seleucid kingdom (Grotius). Rome was terrifying to Christians "both Rome Pagan and Rome Papal." The iron teeth may be generals such as Scipio, Pompey and Caesar. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-7.html
- Wesley ("The Roman empire"), Utley at bible.org (Rome, going by the order of chapters 2, 7 and 8) and Constable (Rome rose and fell slowly; the beast is like no known animal) all agree. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-daniel/ ; https://bible.org/seriespage/daniel-7 ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-7.html
- Matthew Henry: notes that some take the fourth beast as Syria under the Seleucids. Whether it is Syria, Rome, or Syria as a picture of Rome, the passage is meant to comfort persecuted believers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_007.cfm

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: the little horn is a man, though he may stand for a kingdom. His eyes show cunning, and his boastful mouth shows vanity and blasphemy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-7.html
- Constable: "This is evidently Antichrist." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/7-8.html
- Gill: rejects the views that the horn is Titus, the Turks or Antiochus, and says it isn't a single person. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/7.htm
- The identity of the horn is the chapter's main disagreement; see Part 2.

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: the thrones are seats for the Judge's assistants. He thinks Matthew 19:28 explains them better than reading them as angels. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-7.html
- Gill: the Septuagint and Vulgate read "thrones were set up," while some Jewish interpreters read "cast down." The white robe means purity, the woolly hair means wisdom and dignity, and the fiery throne means God's fearsome judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/7.htm
- Wesley: he follows the "cast down" reading: the kingdoms of this world are destroyed by God, who is called Ancient of Days because of his eternal deity. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-daniel/
- Enduring Word: the Ancient of Days is God. Most take him to be the Father, because v. 13 distinguishes him from the Son of Man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-7/
- Matthew Henry: he is called Ancient of Days because he is God from everlasting to everlasting. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_007.cfm

**v. 10**
- Matthew Henry: a river of life flows to God's friends (Revelation 22:1), and a river of fire comes out against his enemies. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_007.cfm
- Gill: compares this scene to the last judgment and the great white throne. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/7.htm
- Simeon: this is not the general judgment but a particular judgment on one persecuting power. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/shh/daniel-7.html
- Ligonier: Daniel sees this from his bed, but the scene itself is the heavenly throne room. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/coming-son-man-unfolding-biblical-eschatology

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: the horn's blasphemy is what brings the judgment. Because the horn's spirit came from the fourth beast, the whole beast is slain and burned. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-7.html
- Wesley: this means the ruin and judgment of antichrist. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-daniel/
- Enduring Word: the boasting matches the Antichrist in Revelation 13:5–6. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-7/

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: the first three beasts lived only as long as God judged fit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/7-12.html
- Gill: those empires faded gradually, and the peoples in them still exist under other governments. The fourth beast, by contrast, will end all at once. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-7.html
- Matthew Henry: they could no longer harm the church, and their lives ran to a limit they couldn't pass. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_007.cfm
- Enduring Word: some nations will carry on into the Millennium. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-7/

**v. 13** (for the different views of what the coming means, see Part 2)
- Ellicott: the title means someone descended from man, but "like" shows he is more than a man. Early Jewish and Christian readers took him to be the Messiah, and Jesus confirmed this by using the title himself (Matthew 24:30). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/7-13.htm
- Gill: "like" is used because he was not yet incarnate. He is not Judas Maccabaeus (Porphyry), the Roman people (Grotius), Israel (Aben Ezra) or the saints (Cocceius). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/7.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/7-13.htm
- Ligonier and The Gospel Coalition: Jesus deliberately identifies with this heavenly figure (Mark 13:26; Matthew 26:63–64). It is his favourite name for himself, used about 80 times. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/son-man-1495 ; https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/jesus-christ-son-man/

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: in biblical Aramaic, "serve" is used only of worshipping God, so the Son of Man is presented as God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-7.html
- Calvin: Christ's dominion means he governs and protects his church for as long as this world lasts, and then in heaven. Barnes: the gospel will come to shape laws and customs. Clarke: Christianity will spread until the end of the world. Henry: the gates of hell won't prevail. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/7-14.html
- The Gospel Coalition: the striking point is that God's kingdom is placed in a man's hands. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/jesus-christ-son-man/

**vv. 15–16**
- Enduring Word: Daniel was troubled because he didn't understand what he saw. The phrase "within my body" shows that the spirit lives in the body. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-7/
- Gill: not knowing the meaning is what hurt him. The person he asked was an angel, and readers shouldn't be ashamed to ask pastors for help. The question and answer both happened inside the vision. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-7.html
- Wesley: he asked an angel. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-daniel/

**v. 17**
- Gill: the kingdoms have earthly origins, which explains what the "sea" means. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-7.html
- Enduring Word: this covers the same ground as chapter 2, but from God's point of view. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-7/
- Utley: the first kingdom had already come. https://bible.org/seriespage/daniel-7

**v. 18**
- Wesley: with Christ as their king, the saints reign with him forever. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-daniel/
- Matthew Henry: Christ's kingdom isn't of this world. The verse points to the saints' spiritual rule over sin and Satan, and to the martyrs' victory over death. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_007.cfm
- Enduring Word: the saints receive the kingdom as a gift at Jesus' return, and never win it themselves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-7/
- The Gospel Coalition (Canada): the kingdom the Son of Man receives becomes his people's inheritance. https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/columns/detrinitate/how-daniel-7-prophecies-of-christs-ascension-in-acts-1-2/

**vv. 19–20**
- Constable: Daniel adds details not given before, including bronze claws and the horn being more prominent than the others, which explains how it could replace three. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/7-20.html
- Gill: reads the horn's bold look as threatening kings with "bulls, anathemas, and interdicts" (that is, papal decrees). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/7-20.html

**vv. 21–22**
- JFB: the persecution lasts until Christ's second coming, so the horn can't belong to the past. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Dan/Dan_007.cfm
- On who "the saints" are, see Part 2.

**v. 23**
- Ellicott: the ten kings exist at the same time, and no explanation so far has worked. We should wait humbly for the fulfilment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-7.html
- Gill: the fourth kingdom is Rome, which lasts until Christ's kingdom comes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-7.html
- Constable: here the beasts are clearly both kings and kingdoms. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-7.html

**v. 24**: see Part 2.

**v. 25**
- Ellicott: the horn can be recognised by three marks: blasphemy, persecution, and attempts, apparently unsuccessful ("intending to"), to overturn all divine and human institutions. "Time, times and half a time" is often read as 3½ years, either literally or as half of a sacred period of seven. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-7.html
- Matthew Henry: he will try to abolish the ordinances of religion. Satan's aim is to wear out the saints, but God will always have a church. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_007.cfm

**v. 26**
- Gill: the Father and Christ sit as judges, with the angels attending. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-7.html
- GotQuestions: the Antichrist is destroyed and Jesus sets up his millennial kingdom. https://www.gotquestions.org/little-horn.html

**v. 27**
- Gill: Christ's spiritual reign comes first, then his personal reign in the Millennium, then eternal glory. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-7.html
- JFB: Daniel saw the whole future blessing as one period. The New Testament separates it into the Millennium and the new heavens and earth. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Dan/Dan_007.cfm

**v. 28**
- Matthew Henry: Daniel kept the matter in his heart, as Mary did, not to hide it but to keep it safe for the church. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_007.cfm
- JFB: the Holy Spirit meant more than Daniel himself understood (1 Peter 1:11–12). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Dan/Dan_007.cfm
- Gill: the "end of the matter" is the end of all events: Christ's kingdom and glory with his people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-7.html

## Part 2 – Where Protestant teachers really differ

**vv. 8, 24–25: Who is the little horn?**
- **The Reformers and the papacy.** Charles Hodge (Reformed) says the Reformers "with one voice" named the papacy as the antichrist of Daniel, Paul and John. Bellarmine wrote a long defence against this. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/hodge/theology3.iv.iii.vi.html
  - Another commentary summarises the range of older views. Oecolampadius saw the Pope in the West and the Turks in the East. Bullinger and the Reformers generally saw the papacy. Junius and Willet saw Antiochus historically and the Antichrist as the later fulfilment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/daniel-7.html
- **Methodist.** Wesley: "Probably either the Turk or the Romish antichrist," and in v. 24, "the Romish antichrist." https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-daniel/
  - Clarke (tagged Wesleyan/Methodist) says Protestants generally see the papacy here. He suggests the three uprooted horns were the exarchate of Ravenna, the Lombards and the state of Rome. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/7-8.html
- **Baptist.** Gill applies the horn to papal Rome. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/7-20.html
- **Restoration Movement.** Coffman records that Alexander Campbell, in debate with Catholic Bishop Purcell, argued that the papacy was Daniel's little horn. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/7-8.html
- **Others with the papal view.** Simeon: the horn is "the Papal Hierarchy." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/shh/daniel-7.html
  - Joseph Mede (cited in Henry's Complete Commentary) says the same, pointing to the pope's claim to change times and laws. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/7-25.html
- **Calvin.** The horn was Julius Caesar and the Caesars after him. It is "little" because Caesar didn't take the title of king. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/7-8.html
  - Hodge notes that Calvin rejected reading "a time" as a year. https://www.monergism.com/antichrist
- **Futurist and dispensational.** Guzik: the horn is a future Antichrist who rises from a restored Roman Empire and rules 3½ years. The ten horns weren't fulfilled in ancient Rome, and Calvin "spiritualizes." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-7/
  - GotQuestions holds the same: a revived Rome, a coalition of ten leaders, and 3½ years matching Revelation 13:5. https://www.gotquestions.org/little-horn.html
  - Constable is slightly different: the present age, with nations that grew out of Rome, is the "10-horned era." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-7.html
- **Charismatic (Sam Storms).** The little horn of chapter 8 is Antiochus, but the horn of chapter 7 is "probably" the end-time antichrist. Making it Antiochus would mean the fourth beast is Greece, not Rome. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-7:1-28-part-ii

**v. 13: When does the Son of Man "come"?**
- **At the Ascension.** Wesley says this is when Christ received his royal investiture. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-daniel/
  - The Geneva notes link it to his ascension into heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/7-13.htm
  - The Gospel Coalition (Canada) ties it to Acts 1–2. https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/columns/detrinitate/how-daniel-7-prophecies-of-christs-ascension-in-acts-1-2/
  - Ligonier stresses that the coming is *to* God in heaven, not from heaven to earth. It contrasts this with the dispensational view, which places it at the Second Coming. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/coming-son-man-unfolding-biblical-eschatology
- **At the Second Coming.** JFB says the title is always linked to his return. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/7-13.htm
- **A symbol, not a literal event.** Barnes reads the scene as a picture of world events and says it isn't the last judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/7-13.htm

**vv. 18, 21–22, 27: Who are "the saints"?**
- Chuck Smith: since the Antichrist defeats them, they can't be the church. They are redeemed Israel during the Tribulation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/7-14.html
- Henry (spiritual victories) and Wesley (believers reigning with Christ) read them as the church. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_007.cfm ; https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-daniel/

## Part 3 – Other views

**The critical (Maccabean) reading, vv. 5–8, 25.**
- Ellicott's excursus describes this view, which goes back to Porphyry and has modern supporters. The fourth beast is Greece and the horn is Antiochus Epiphanes, in whose time the book was supposedly written. The bear is Media (its ribs are three satrapies), and the leopard is Persia.
- Ellicott rejects it for several reasons. The time periods don't match (2,300 days in chapter 8 against "time, times" here). Greece absorbed the nations it conquered rather than crushing them. And Daniel doesn't present Media as a separate empire. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/7.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-7.html
- Guzik says the Median view exists only to remove Rome and predictive prophecy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-7/
- Walvoord (bible.org) explains why the critics hold it, and argues that the horn of chapter 8 comes from a different context. https://bible.org/seriespage/chapter-7-daniel%E2%80%99s-vision-future-world-history
- Storms notes that Antiochus banned Jewish festivals and the Sabbath, which fits "change the appointed times" in v. 25. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-7:1-28-part-ii
- The Expositor's Bible (a Spanish translation on StudyLight) treats the author as writing while the persecuting horn was in power. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/teb/daniel-7.html

**v. 13: Is the Son of Man a group?**
- The Cambridge Bible says "the Son of man" is an untenable translation; the original is indefinite. Because the explanation in vv. 18, 22 and 27 gives the kingdom to the saints, the figure most likely stands for the ideal people of God.
- Keil and Delitzsch report that some read the figure as Israel, though Jewish and Christian interpreters generally take it as the Messiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/7-13.htm

**Catholic, v. 13.** The Catholic Encyclopedia says many non-Catholics read the figure as the messianic kingdom. Nothing prevents it from meaning the Messianic King above all. It notes that the Book of Enoch already read it as the Messiah. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/son-of-man

**Early church and Catholic, v. 8.** The early church believed the little horn and Paul's "man of sin" were the same Antichrist (Justin Martyr is cited). Futurists and Roman Catholic writers expect an Antichrist still to come. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/daniel-7.html
